text: Given an integer array, return the length of the longest turbulent subarray. A subarray is turbulent if the comparison sign flips between each pair of neighbors: bigger, smaller, bigger, and so on.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the subarray is contiguous. I look at each step between neighbors, and each step is either up or down. The steps must strictly alternate: up, down, up, or down, up, down. It can start either way. And if two neighbors are equal, that step is neither up nor down, so it breaks the run. Is that right?
Yes. Strict alternation, either direction, and equal neighbors break it.

Okay. Then a few small facts. One element alone always counts, so the answer is at least one. Any two different neighbors make a length-two run, one step. And the only thing that matters is the direction of each step, not how big it is. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to four times ten to the fourth elements, and each value is between zero and ten to the ninth.

Got it. So I want one pass. The values go up to ten to the ninth, which still fits in an int. I'll keep that in mind, because it matters if I ever multiply two differences. Let me run through the example: nine, four, two, ten, seven, eight, eight, one, nine. The steps are: down, down, up, down, up, equal, down, up. The best run is index one to five — four, two, ten, seven, eight. Four above two, two below ten, ten above seven, seven below eight. That's down, up, down, up, so length five. It can't grow left, because nine to four is down again. And it can't grow right, because eight to eight is equal. The other example, four, eight, twelve, sixteen, only goes up, so the best is any one step, length two. And a single one hundred is just one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every start and every end, and check if the part in between is turbulent. That's cubic time, or quadratic if I grow each start until it breaks. It's correct, and I'd keep it as a brute force to test against. But at forty thousand elements it's too slow. This problem reminds me of the two-running-Kadanes pattern: a running best ending at each index, kept as two coupled values — like a running max and a running min, because one state swaps into the other. Here it's the same shape. I keep two runs ending at index i: one whose last step goes up, and one whose last step goes down. An up step can only extend a run that ended going down, and the other way around. So the two values feed each other.

Here's the plan. I keep three numbers, all starting at one: the best length anywhere, a running length for the run ending here whose last step goes up, and one whose last step goes down. Then for each index from one onward, I first copy both running values into previous-up and previous-down — copy first, that matters. If this element is bigger than the one before, the step goes up, so the up run becomes the previous down run plus one; otherwise it resets to one. If this element is smaller, the down run becomes the previous up run plus one; otherwise it resets to one. Then I refresh the best with both. If the step is equal, neither compare fires, so both reset to one — the equal case is handled for free. The key rule is the cross. If this step goes up, the run before it must have ended going down, and the other way around. Whichever direction this step is not, that value resets to one, because a run whose last step goes the other way can only be the current element alone. One thing worth flagging — the start value is one, not zero, for all three. Let me walk through that. One element alone is a valid run. If I started the best at zero, a single-element array never enters the loop and returns zero. And if the reset value were zero instead of one, every run would come out one too short — example one would give four. There's a trade-off here. I could also use one counter: if the sign of the step flips, add one; if it's equal, go to one; otherwise go to two. That also works. But then I need to compare the current step with the previous step, and the easy way to write that is multiplying two differences, which can overflow. I'll come back to that. The two-counter version only uses greater-than and less-than, and it reads like the definition. So I'll go with that. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up — and I'll talk through it rather than read it line by line. I take the array's size, and set the best, the up run, and the down run all to one. Then one loop from index one to the end. Inside, I first save both current values as previous-up and previous-down. Then the up run: if this element is greater than the one before, it becomes previous-down plus one, otherwise one. The down run: if this element is less than the one before, it becomes previous-up plus one, otherwise one. And the best takes the max of all three. After the loop I return the best. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the two copies, previous-up and previous-down. They look extra, but they're needed for correctness. Here's a version I almost wrote: the same two ternary lines, but reading the running values directly instead of the copies. The problem is the second line. It reads the up run after the first line overwrote it. And on a down step, the first line always sets the up run to one, because the step isn't up. So the second line always gives one plus one, which is two. Every down step cuts the chain back to two. On example one, it returns three instead of five. The first wrong step is index four: the down run should be three plus one, four, but it becomes two. The smallest input that breaks it is zero, one, zero: it returns two, but the answer is three. And it's sneaky: the all-up example and the single-element example still pass. That version can never return more than three. Copying both old values first, before I write either one, fixes it. Also, I only compare with greater-than and less-than. I don't multiply the two neighboring differences and check the sign in int. Each difference fits, but the product doesn't. On zero, a billion, zero, it's ten to the ninth times negative ten to the ninth, which overflows. That's undefined behavior, and in my test it printed garbage. A long-long cast fixes it, but not needing it is cleaner.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use example one: nine, four, two, ten, seven, eight, eight, one, nine. Expected output is five. At index zero, all three start at one. The first two steps go down, down — the down run gets to two, but a second down in a row starts over, because the previous up run was just one. Then at index three, two to ten goes up, and it picks up the previous down run: two plus one, three. Index four goes down and picks up that three: four. Now the key row, index five. Seven to eight goes up, so the up run becomes the previous down run plus one — four plus one, five. That four came from index four, where ten to seven went down and took the previous up run, three, plus one. So the chain is passed back and forth: two, then three, then four, then five. That's the run four, two, ten, seven, eight — index one to five. Then at index six, eight to eight is equal, so both reset to one. After that the runs only reach three, so the best stays at five. That matches. Also look at index two: two down steps in a row. The down run goes back to two, because the previous up run was one. Same direction twice means start over from the last pair. Let's also test with corner cases. Four, eight, twelve, sixteen gives two: every step is up, so the down run is always one and the up run is always two. A single element gives one — the loop never runs, which is why the best starts at one. Zero, one, zero gives three: up then down, and the almost-written version returns two here. One, two, one, two, two, one gives four — the run grows to four, then the equal pair resets both. All equal, like four fives, gives one. If I had used greater-or-equal instead of strictly greater, two equal elements would give two, and example one would give six. And the big one: forty thousand elements alternating zero and a billion gives the whole array, forty thousand. All equal gives one. Strictly increasing gives two.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear. One pass, and each step is two compares and a max. The space complexity is constant — just a few integers. In the worst case it's still exactly n minus one steps, with no early exit. At forty thousand elements, the alternating array takes about twenty-eight microseconds. The counters never go above n, and I never do math on the values, only compares, so there's no overflow anywhere. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the brute force on lots of arrays. I ran over two hundred twenty-three thousand cases, every small array plus random large ones, with zero mismatches. That check matters here. The almost-written version passes two of the three official examples. But on every array of length one to seven with values zero to two, it fails nineteen hundred twenty-three out of about three thousand three hundred. And any answer of four or more is always wrong. A few hand-picked tests can miss that. A brute-force check won't.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You split the state into two runs, last step up and last step down, and saw that they cross-feed: each one extends the other. You explained why the previous copies are a correctness need, not style — without them every down step cuts to two, and zero, one, zero breaks it. And you avoided the difference-product trick because it overflows an int at a billion. Good work.
